papers.title: Dynamic $(Δ+1)$-Coloring Against an Adaptive Adversary: Faster, Simpler, Worst-Case, and Bounded Recourse
papers.abstract: We study fully dynamic $(Δ+1)$-coloring against an adaptive adversary. Behnezhad, Rajaraman, and Wasim (SODA 2025) gave the first algorithm with $\tilde O(n^{8/9})$ amortized update time, later improved to $\tilde O(n^{2/3})$ by Flin and Halldórsson (ICALP 2025). We give a fully dynamic $(Δ+1)$-coloring algorithm with $\tilde O(\sqrt n)$ \textbf{worst-case} update time. Unlike previous algorithms, it avoids sparse-dense decompositions and relies only on elementary data structures, resulting in a short self-contained algorithm and analysis. Moreover, it avoids global recoloring, resulting in a worst-case recourse of $3$.

papers.title: Tight Inapproximability for Generalized Circuits
papers.abstract: Generalized circuits are a fundamental tool for establishing PPAD-hardness and membership of approximate equilibrium problems. Despite their importance, the complexity of finding approximate solutions has remained unresolved for a wide range of approximation parameters. We settle this question by establishing a tight threshold at $\varepsilon=1/6$. Specifically, we prove that $\varepsilon$-GCircuit is PPAD-complete for every constant $0<\varepsilon<1/6$, even when restricted to four gate types, and polynomial-time solvable for every constant $\varepsilon\ge1/6$. This closes the gap between the previously known hardness bound of $1/10$ and the polynomial-time solvability bound of $1/2$. We further investigate the relaxation in which a fraction $δ$ of the gates may be violated. We establish polynomial-time solvability of $(\varepsilon,δ)$-GCircuit for every constant $\varepsilon>0$ and $δ>1/5$, and of the fan-out-one formulations of $δ$-Pure-Circuit for every constant $δ>1/8$. These results follow from a decomposition theorem for directed graphs of maximum in-degree two and establish that the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture cannot be true for the aforementioned values of $\varepsilon$ and $δ$, unless PPAD = P. To showcase the contribution of our positive results, we apply them to a variety of problems in algorithmic game theory, including public goods games, financial networks, Bayesian, polymatrix, and graphical games, and obtain improved approximation guarantees.

papers.title: Hardness Amplification for Approximate Nash Equilibrium with Constantly Many Players
papers.abstract: For every fixed $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ and $η\in[0,1)$, we prove that computing an $(\varepsilon,η)$-weak approximate Nash equilibrium requires quasipolynomial time assuming deterministic PPAD-ETH, even in symmetric binary-payoff games with a constant number of players. The games are given by complete payoff tables, and the player count depends only on the tolerances. The weak approximate Nash equilibrium allows at most an $η$ fraction of players to gain more than $\varepsilon$ by deviating unilaterally. The main technical result is an unconditional error-amplification reduction from bimatrix games. For every fixed $δ\in(0,1)$, it transforms a rational bimatrix game with payoffs in $[0,1]$ into a symmetric binary-payoff game with a polynomial-size complete table and a player count depending only on $δ,\varepsilon,η$. Every $(\varepsilon,η)$-weak approximate equilibrium of the constructed game yields a $δ$-approximate Nash equilibrium of the bimatrix game. Construction and recovery take polynomial time in their explicit inputs. Combining this reduction with the bimatrix hardness result of Rubinstein [FOCS 16] gives a deterministic worst-case running-time lower bound of $N^{(\log N)^{1-o(1)}}$, where $N$ is the constructed table's binary encoding length.

papers.title: High Precision Multiplicative-Error Approximation of $\#$SAC$^1$ Functions in Logspace Uniform AC$^1$
papers.abstract: Cheng and Wang (CCC' 24) showed that BPL is contained in logspace uniform AC$^1$ (denoted as L-AC$^1$). We upgrade their result by showing that $\#$SAC functions (i.e., functions computed by logspace-uniform polynomial-size positive semi-unbounded arithmetic circuits) can be approximately computed by L-AC circuits with high precision. In particular, approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions can be computed in L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Previously, approximations of $\#$SAC$^1$ functions are known to be in $\mathsf{NC}^2$ via its exact computation given by Vinay (CCC' 91). A main corollary of our result is that BPAuxPDMs and Read-$k$-BPL are computable by L-AC$^1$ with multiplicative error $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$. Notice that multiplicative error approximations can be used directly to decide non-deterministic computations. So our L-AC$^1$ circuits can automatically be used to decide non-deterministic AuxPDMs and hence NL. We note that recently OpenAI announced that BPL $=$ L. Even if we only consider derandomizing BPL, our L-AC$^1$ computation has the advantage that the error can be $2^{-\mathrm{poly}\log n}$ and can be multiplicative.

papers.title: Regularizing the Veto Core
papers.abstract: The metric distortion framework asks voting rules to elect a candidate close to the voters using only their rankings. SimultaneousPluralityVeto elects from the plurality veto core and achieves the optimal worst-case distortion of 3, but it is not Pareto-efficient: it can declare a tie between two candidates even when every voter prefers one of them. Removing Pareto-dominated candidates afterward would break the convexity of tied winner sets. We instead introduce regularization, which adds a small $\varepsilon$ to every candidate's weight, restoring Pareto-efficiency. To study its effect on distortion, we introduce the rank score veto core, whose candidate weights come from a positional scoring vector $\mathbf{s}$, and prove that its distortion lies in $[1 + 2(||\mathbf{s}|| - s_m),\, 1 + 2||\mathbf{s}||]$; we conjecture that the lower bound is tight. A fixed $\varepsilon$ can increase distortion, but letting $\varepsilon$ depend on the number of voters preserves the distortion guarantee of the original veto core. Regularized SimultaneousPluralityVeto thus has optimal distortion, is Pareto-efficient, and has convex tied winner sets, resolving an open question of Kızılkaya and Kempe.

papers.title: Internalizing Chain-of-thought into Looped Transformers
papers.abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) enables constant-bit-size transformers to perform general-purpose computation through generated tokens (Li and Wang, 2025a), whereas looped transformers carry out the same computation by recurrence in hidden states (latent thought). We construct a family of constant-bit-size looped transformers that interpolates between CoT and latent thought. For a prescribed loop count $L=L(n)$ and a fixed integer $k\ge1$ satisfying $s(n)^{1/k}=Ω(L)$, our transformer simulates a time-$t(n)$, space-$s(n)$ Turing machine using a context window of $O(s(n)/L)$ and $O(t(n)s(n)^{1/k}/L)$ generated tokens, reducing both resources by a factor of $L$ relative to the corresponding unlooped queue-machine simulation. The construction also holds with softmax attention at constant bit-size, under the finite-precision kernel specified in this paper.

papers.title: Solving Classes of Linear Programs with Strongly Polynomial Straight Line Complexity in Strongly Polynomial Time
papers.abstract: Recently, Allamigeon, Dadush, Loho, Natura, and Végh (ADLNV, SICOMP 2025) introduced an interior point method for linear programs whose number of iterations is bounded by the so-called straight line complexity (SLC) of the instance. This yields a strongly polynomial bound on the number of iterations of the corresponding interior point algorithm for broad classes of linear programs. In particular, in the companion paper we give a strongly polynomial straight line complexity bound for two-variable-per-inequality linear programs. However, in order to obtain a strongly polynomial algorithm for these classes, one also needs to address two important technical issues: initialization and bit-complexity bounds. Standard IPM initialization techniques either require numerical estimates that cannot be obtained in the strongly polynomial model, or involve modifying the instance in ways that do not preserve the geometry of the original LP, potentially affecting the SLC. In this work, we present an initialization framework for interior point methods for linear programming, along with a rounding procedure that ensures the continued feasibility of the IPM. We develop a multistage scheme in which each stage can be initialized in strongly polynomial time given the output of the previous stage. Additionally, we address the challenge of controlling the bit complexity of each iterate throughout the algorithm. To this end, we show that it is possible to represent iterates as low-complexity convex combinations of vertices and extreme rays. Our combinatorial rounding step is independent of the algorithm in ADLNV 2025, and can be applied more broadly in the context of path-following methods.
papers.comment: This paper is based on the STOC 2024 proceedings paper "A strongly polynomial algorithm for linear programs with at most two nonzero entries per row or column'' , and includes the full details of the initialization framework and the bit complexity arguments

papers.title: The rank of the random $k$-XORSAT matrix beyond satisfiability
papers.abstract: The random $k$-XORSAT matrix is an $m\times n$ random matrix $\mathbf A$ over $\mathbb F_2$ that represents a random instance of the $k$-XORSAT problem. Each row of $\mathbf A$ contains precisely $k\geq3$ non-zero entries in random positions. The rows are drawn independently. The matrix $\mathbf A$ is known to have full row rank for $m/n$ below the random $k$-XORSAT satisfiability threshold, which is known explicitly [Dubois, Mandler~2002; Pittel, Sorkin~2016]. Motivated by a problem from quantum game theory and refining a result of Cooper, Frieze and Pegden (2019), we determine the limiting distribution of the rank of $\mathbf A$ beyond the satisfiability threshold.

papers.title: Integer Programing: An Algorithm with Exponent Linear in the Dimension
papers.abstract: We study integer programs in standard form $\min\{\mathbf{c}^{\mathsf{T}}\mathbf{x}:A\mathbf{x}=\mathbf{b},\ \mathbf{l}\leq\mathbf{x}\leq\mathbf{u},\ \mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{Z}^n\}$, where $A\in\mathbb{Z}^{d\times n}$ and all entries of $\mathbf{b},\mathbf{c},\mathbf{l},\mathbf{u}$ are integers. Let $N$ be an upper bound on the absolute values of the entries of $A$. We give a deterministic algorithm running in time \[ \operatorname{poly}(L_{\rm in})+ f(d)\,N^{O(d)}\bigl(1+\log(c_{\max}+1)\bigr)^{O(1)}, \] where $c_{\max}$ bounds the absolute values of the costs and $L_{\rm in}$ is the input length. Prior to our work, the best known running time was $N^{O(d^2)}$ [Eisenbrand \& Weismantel'20], and it has been a fundamental open problem whether the exponent $O(d^2)$ can be improved to one linear in $d$. We answer this question affirmatively.

papers.title: Orienting mixed graphs for reachability pairs: When the all pairs setting is easier than the general one
papers.abstract: Given a mixed graph $G$ and an ordered pair $(u,v)$ of vertices in $V(G)$, we say that an orientation $\vec{G}$ of $G$ satisfies $(u,v)$ if $v$ is reachable from $u$ in $\vec{G}$. We consider problems in which we seek orientations that satisfy a maximum number of pairs. We distinguish between two different problems. In the most general problem called Fixed Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (FPRO), a multiset $P$ of ordered pairs of vertices in $V(G)$ comes with the input. In the more restricted problem All Pairs Maximum Mixed Reachability Orientation (APRO), $P$ contains exactly one copy of every ordered pair of distinct vertices in $V(G)$. We compare the computational complexity of FPRO and APRO in two ways: First, we show that both FPRO and APRO behave similarly when it comes to approximation. Namely, they both admit an asymptotic approximation, but are unlikely to admit a constant factor approximation. Then, we consider the parameterization with respect to the treewidth of the underlying graph of the input mixed graph. We show that here the complexities of FPRO and APRO differ significantly. While it is well-known that FPRO is NP-hard even when this parameter is 1, we show that APRO is XP with respect to this parameter. On the other hand, we give a $W[1]$-hardness result for APRO.

papers.title: Hadamard Transforms for Dimension Reduction
papers.abstract: Using the Hadamard matrix for dimension reduction can accelerate the computation due to the fast Hadamard transform. However, the previous target dimension bounds in terms of the Gaussian width depend on the ambient dimension. In this paper, we obtain the following ambient dimension free bound using three Hadamard-diagonal blocks. Let $H\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be the normalized Walsh-Hadamard matrix, and let $D_1,D_2,D_3\in\mathbb R^{d\times d}$ be independent Rademacher diagonal matrices. We prove that for any symmetric set $T\subset \mathbb{S}^{d-1}$, \[ \mathbb P\left\{\sup_{\boldsymbol t\in T}\big|\frac dm\|P_ΩHD_3HD_2HD_1\boldsymbol t\|_2^2-1\big|\le\varepsilon\right\} \ge1-δ\] whenever \[ m\gtrsim\varepsilon^{-2}w(T)^2\log^2\frac eδ\,\log^4\!\left(e+\frac{w(T)}\varepsilon\log\frac eδ\right). \] Here $w(T)$ is the Gaussian width of $T$, and $Ω$ is a set of $m$ distinct coordinates chosen uniformly. This is the first ambient dimension free bound on the target dimension using Hadamard transforms, for an arbitrary symmetric set in terms of its Gaussian width. We also prove that it is impossible to obtain an ambient dimension free bound for an arbitrary set in terms of its Gaussian width using two Hadamard-diagonal blocks.

papers.title: A Tight Oracle Threshold for \(k\)-Submodular Maximization
papers.abstract: We prove that, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), a \((\frac{k}{2k-1}+\varepsilon)\)-approximation algorithm for maximizing monotone \(k\)-submodular functions requires exponentially many value-oracle queries. This improves the \(\frac{k+1}{2k}\) oracle bound of Iwata, Tanigawa, and Yoshida. Their \(\frac{k}{2k-1}\)-approximation algorithm therefore gives the exact threshold in the monotone setting. For \(k\ge5\), our bound also matches, up to an arbitrarily small loss, Aggarwal's recent approximation guarantee for non-monotone \(k\)-submodular maximization.

papers.title: Exact minimum Birkhoff decompositions of doubly stochastic matrices with finite precision
papers.abstract: The minimum Birkhoff decomposition problem asks for a representation of a doubly stochastic matrix as a convex combination of as few permutation matrices as possible. This NP-hard problem arises in the scheduling of switches in data centers and satellite systems, in random assignments in economics and in the statistics of rankings. We consider doubly stochastic matrices whose entries are given with a fixed number of decimal digits and look for exact decompositions whose weights have the same precision. We propose a parallel method with three parts. For matrices built from few permutation matrices, the first part reads the weights from the frequencies of the entries and places them on the matrix positions by a rule that, given the correct weights, never fixes a position wrongly. The second part computes lower bounds from pairs of rows or columns, which remain valid for real weights, and from certificates of a satisfiability solver. For matrices built from many permutation matrices, the third part runs a beam search over steps that each make at least one entry zero. On 375 test instances with up to 100 rows, the method proves optimality for 208 instances, and 197 of these proofs also hold for real weights. Of the 190 instances built from few permutation matrices, 187 are solved to proven optimality, 180 of them within one second. Compared with the best exact decompositions known before, the new decompositions are shorter for 278 instances and never longer.

papers.title: Ski Rental with Uniform Stochastic Signals
papers.abstract: Ski rental is one of the most fundamental online problems, where an agent repeatedly decides whether it should continue renting for a service, or buy it at a one-time fixed cost. In classic online analysis, an adversary may freely select any arbitrary time horizon $t$ after which the instance terminates, hence leading to strong competitive ratio lower bounds of 2 (deterministic) and $e/(e-1)$ (randomized). We consider a novel but natural model aiming at limiting the adversary's power without degrading its flexibility. A stochastic signal, containing no information apart from its arrival time, is transmitted to the algorithm at a time drawn from a known distribution scaled to $[0,t]$. This framework allows us to account for visible effects of the adversary's choice to the algorithm. Focusing as a first step on uniform distributions, we show that the best possible competitive ratios are approximately $1.478$ (deterministic) and $1.438$ (randomized). Surprisingly, simplistic deterministic strategies already achieve a performance of $1.489$.

papers.title: Invitation to torso parameters of annotated graphs
papers.abstract: An annotated graph is a pair $(G,S)$, where $G$ is a graph and $S$ is a subset of vertices of $G$. We present a unified approach for definitions of annotated versions of classical graph parameters such as treewidth, pathwidth, treedepth, etc. A generic way to incorporate a distinguished set of vertices into a graph parameter is via torsos. Given a graph $G$ and a subset $S'\subseteq V(G)$, we define $\mathrm{torso}_G(S')$ to be the graph with vertex set $S'$ in which distinct vertices $u,v\in S'$ are adjacent if and only if there exists a $u$-$v$ path in $G$ whose internal vertices lie outside $S'$. Now let $\mathrm{p}$ be any graph parameter. For an annotated graph $(G,S)$, we define the torso $\mathrm{p}$ of $(G,S)$ by \[\mathrm{p}(G,S) = \min\{\mathrm{p}(\mathrm{torso}_G(S')) \mid S \subset S' \subset V(G)\}.\] For a minor-closed class of annotated graphs $\mathcal{C}$, we discuss equivalent conditions for $\mathrm{p}(G,S)$ bounded for all $(G,S)\in\mathcal{C}$ in terms of annotated graphs excluded in $\mathcal{C}$. In many cases, we collect known results from the literature. We include two new arguments for $\mathrm{p}$ being the $2$-treedepth and the feedback vertex number. Among other statements, we also include a variant of the Erdős-Pósa property for annotated cycles. We propose some new research directions.

papers.title: Game of Phones: Harnessing Game Theory and LLMs in 'Bot Wars' to Counteract Phone Scams
papers.abstract: Phone scams impose substantial and growing costs on individuals and financial systems worldwide, yet existing countermeasures impose no resource cost on perpetrators. Strategic scam-baiting, in which automated agents engage scammers to deplete their operational capacity, offers a proactive alternative but requires dynamic strategy adaptation that static systems cannot provide. We introduce a game-theoretic framework enabling LLMs to learn effective counter-strategies through in-context experience without fine-tuning. The framework models scammer-baiter interactions as a two-player game with empirically grounded strategies and utility functions, using Nash equilibrium as a formal benchmark for evaluating learned behaviour. Across 300 simulated dialogues and three LLM architectures, adaptive strategy selection achieves 28.9-79.7% closer alignment to Nash equilibrium than non-adaptive baselines. The code and an annotated dataset of 300 dialogues with turn-level strategy labels and utility scores are released at https://github.com/nardinebasta/GameofPhones_/ .

papers.journal_ref: Lecture Notes in Computer Science, vol. 16949 (2027) 395-411

papers.title: Single-level reformulations for network pricing under Wardrop equilibrium with separable affine costs
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of setting tolls on a subset of the arcs of a congested network so as to maximize the revenue of a network authority, anticipating that users route according to a Wardrop equilibrium. This problem is naturally cast as a bilevel program in which the leader sets tolls while the followers respond by choosing an equilibrium routing. We focus on the important special case of separable affine arc cost functions. Under this assumption, Wardrop equilibria admit Beckmann's convex characterization, from which we derive three new single-level reformulations of the bilevel problem, exploiting both Beckmann's formulation and its dual: an arc-based formulation, which we solve exactly, and two path-based formulations, solved by column-and-constraint generation. Beyond the reformulations, we further derive from Beckmann's potential an upper bound on the optimal revenue that can be used to certify optimality gaps across all formulations. An extensive computational study on instances derived from the Sioux Falls and Eastern Massachusetts networks compares our formulations with the recent mixed-integer nonlinear formulation of Beck, Labbé and Schmidt. The arc-based formulation solves substantially more instances to proven optimality (within a time limit of 1800 s) than this formulation and, unlike it, returns a feasible solution on every instance. It remains effective on the largest, 74-node network, on which the formulation of Beck et al. solves none. The magnitude of the upper bounds on the tolls proves to be a major driver of tractability: the genuinely hard core of the benchmark emerges once the regulatory cap on tolls is removed. The two path-based formulations, used as heuristics, return a solution within one percent of the optimum on every instance whose optimal value is known, often in seconds where exact formulations reach the time limit.

papers.title: Sustainable and Envy-free Multi-Period Allocation
papers.abstract: Allocating renewable resources fairly requires accounting for how present decisions affect future availability. We introduce Sustainable and Envy-Free Multi-Period Allocation, in which agents are assigned over multiple periods to renewable resources whose quantities evolve over time according to renewal functions. An allocation must respect viability and capacity constraints while being envy-free over the whole time horizon. We study the computational and parameterized complexity of finding such allocations, with a focus on the three dimensions of the problem: the numbers of agents, resources, and periods. We show that finding such an allocation is NP-hard already for unary encoding and any single one of them being fixed to a constant. Whether two small dimensions suffice for tractability depends on the pair, the class of renewal functions, and the numerical encoding. For few resources and periods, binary-encoded instances remain hard in general, whereas unary encoding yields XP-time algorithms. For few resources and agents, binary-encoded instances also remain hard in general but become XP-time solvable when all renewal functions are translations. Few agents and periods yield fixed-parameter tractability, but no polynomial kernel under standard complexity assumptions.

papers.title: Controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable and not recursively enumerable
papers.abstract: Sontag conjectured in 1988 that global controllability of polynomial control systems with rational coefficients is undecidable, but that the controllable systems form a recursively enumerable set. We prove the first part of the conjecture and disprove the second. For every homogeneous polynomial vector field $F$ of odd degree with rational coefficients, we construct an explicit polynomial control system $Σ_F$, with one more state than $F$, that is globally controllable if and only if the origin is \emph{not} globally asymptotically stable for $\dot x=F(x)$. By a recent result, the homogeneous polynomial vector fields with a globally asymptotically stable origin form a set that is recursively enumerable but not decidable. Consequently, global controllability of polynomial systems is undecidable, and the controllable polynomial systems are not recursively enumerable. The same conclusions hold for systems of the form $\dotξ=f(ξ)+Bu$ with a polynomial drift and a constant input matrix.

papers.title: Bidirectionality is Necessary in Cellular Machines for Exact-Arrival Multi-Agent Path Finding
papers.abstract: On ranked directed acyclic graphs coupled by vertex conflicts we study exact-arrival multi-agent path finding (departure and arrival pinned in place and time) posed as a distributed output task: every cell must emit its own bit of a valid joint path-support mask. The machines are cellular: one automaton per cell, state factored over cells, communication only along a fixed local fabric, synchronous rounds, a query-independent output round, no central decoder, and a per-topology transition code. "Necessary" here means: on an explicit hard topology, over all its feasible queries, no universally correct local-only architecture can renounce either temporal orientation; with global flags, impossibility becomes a bandwidth-round trade-off. The class is not vacuous: a flooding machine solves every instance in as many rounds as the diameter of the local fabric. The bound survives two concessions: we supply every agent's exact individual cavity, which alone solves the single-agent problem in zero rounds and makes the single-agent direction theorem vacuous; and we allow $k$ one-bit global aggregate flags. On a twelve-cell, two-agent, depth-three topology no forward-only machine with $k=0$ is correct on two feasible queries, for any number of rounds; the time-reversed topology does the same to backward-only machines. Placing $p$ copies side by side gives, for forward-only machines, $J_R+kR\ge p$ at constant depth, where $J_R$ measures how much of the query reaches the targets' cones and is $0$ here. A backward-only machine solves that family in constant rounds and a flag-streaming one in $\lceil p/k\rceil+O(1)$, so the bound is tight in order; on the composite family neither orientation can be renounced. The finite lemmas of the gadget and the pair-invariance contradictions are checked in Lean 4; the semantic bridge, the cone lemma and the counting are paper proofs. We report no benchmarks.
papers.comment: 33 pages. Ancillary files: Lean 4 development for the finite gadget (theoremA.lean), exhaustive check scripts with frozen expected outputs, reproduction README and clean-run log. Companion paper: "Stability Certifies Validity: Amoeba-Inspired Rule Systems for SAT and Single-Agent Trajectory Constraints, Machine-Checked in Lean 4"

papers.title: Constructive Arithmetic Regularity for Abelian Groups
papers.abstract: The arithmetic regularity lemma of Green is a fundamental tool in additive combinatorics, providing a decomposition of arbitrary subsets of finite Abelian groups into pseudorandom pieces with respect to Fourier analysis. Over the years, it has found numerous applications in combinatorics, property testing, and theoretical computer science. However, Green's proof is existential, and many algorithmic applications require an efficient procedure for constructing the underlying regular decomposition. De, Nadimpalli, and Servedio (SODA 2022) developed a query-efficient constructive regularity framework over $\mathbb{F}_2^n$ and explicitly raised the problem of extending their dimension-independent sumset-estimation algorithm to other finite Abelian groups. In this work, we resolve this question for finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. We develop the first constructive version of Green's {\em Arithmetic Regularity Lemma} in this general setting. Given oracle access to a subset of the group, our algorithm computes an implicit description of a regular decomposition together with an oracle representation of a structured subset satisfying the guarantees of Green's lemma. The algorithm runs in time and query complexity polynomial in the regularity parameters and the tower bound, while remaining independent of the size of the ambient group. As applications, we obtain efficient algorithms for removing linear configurations and approximately counting linear images, including weighted sumsets and suitable matrix systems of Cauchy--Schwarz complexity one, over finite Abelian groups of constant torsion. Our results provide a unified algorithmic framework extending dimension-independent constructive arithmetic regularity and its applications beyond $\mathbb{F}_2^n$.

papers.title: PSPACE-Completeness of the Reachability Relation of Robust Dynamical Systems
papers.abstract: Dynamical systems are a widely used model of computation and an intuitive representation of many natural phenomena in many applied fields. The last decades have seen an impressive use of computers in studying and analysing them, with several visible theoretical breakthroughs. The question of reachability for dynamical systems is central: given two points, is there a trajectory between them in the dynamical system? Reachability, in particular over the reals, is undecidable in the general case: it is only computably enumerable, even under reasonable hypotheses, e.g. for a computable dynamics in general. But it is known to become decidable, and even lies in PSPACE, under suitably quantified robustness assumptions. In this paper, we focus on PSPACE-completeness results over the reals, in the sense of computable analysis, regarding discrete-time and continuous-time robust dynamical systems. We prove that, under some additional and rather reasonable hypotheses, the reachability relation becomes even PSPACE-complete for both classical and second-order complexity second-order complexity, for an adapted notion of reduction. As a side-effect, we also prove an improvement of an algebraic Ordinary Differential Equations-based characterisation of PSPACE, removing one of the base functions of the algebra. By doing so, we link results from dynamical systems and complexity over the reals, including the models of computable analysis and second-order complexity.

papers.title: A simplified proof of the FPRAS for counting perfect matchings
papers.abstract: We give a simplified, self-contained proof of OpenAI's FPRAS for counting perfect matchings in general graphs. As in the original proof, we use a restricted Poincaré inequality for two matchings to sample weighted perfect matchings and estimate their total weight. We simplify the proof of this inequality by isolating parts of alternating cycles directly on the original vertex set and controlling the resulting error terms. This avoids the auxiliary vertices and tree constructions used in the original proof. The argument preserves the required parameter bounds and yields the same FPRAS guarantee.

papers.title: Capacitated Line Aggregation with Maximum Delay
papers.abstract: We study capacitated line aggregation with per-batch maximum delay. Requests arrive over time at locations on a rooted half-line and are served in instantaneous batches of at most $k$ requests. Each batch pays the distance to its farthest request plus the waiting time of its oldest request. The objective is to minimize the total cost. We give a deterministic online algorithm with competitive ratio $36+12\sqrt3$. The algorithm uses a Next Fit idea along paths of nested time intervals: it assigns a new group to an existing batch when a path-load test permits, and opens a new batch otherwise. The path load controls both capacity and the cost of opening new batches. Randomizing the common scale improves the expected competitive ratio to $(18+6\sqrt3)/\ln2$ against an oblivious adversary. Both guarantees extend to arbitrary indivisible request sizes. We also study capacitated LAD in the learning-augmented model. Advice revealed at its service times allows $(1+ε)$-consistency against every complete feasible advice schedule and $O(ε^{-2})$-robustness. The analysis charges repeated switches to successive decreases in the remaining advice cost.

papers.title: Euclidean Embeddings of Acyclic Hypergraph Line Metrics
papers.abstract: We study Euclidean embeddings of higher-order line metrics arising from hypergraphs. For a fixed threshold \(s\geq 1\), the \(s\)-line graph \(L_s(H)\) has one vertex for each hyperedge of \(H\), with two hyperedges adjacent when they intersect in at least \(s\) vertices; its shortest-path metric is the native \(s\)-line metric. In the unrestricted setting, every finite graph occurs as the \(s\)-line graph of some hypergraph, so the worst-case Euclidean distortion is \(Θ(\log n)\). We show that \(α\)-acyclicity yields a sharp improvement to \(Θ(\sqrt{\log\log n})\). Although the canonical join tree of an \(α\)-acyclic hypergraph may have arbitrarily large stretch relative to the native metric, we prove that for every \(s\), the \(s\)-line graphs of \(α\)-acyclic hypergraphs are exactly the dually chordal graphs. Using their constant-factor spanning-tree approximations together with classical tree-embedding bounds, we obtain an \(O(\sqrt{\log\log n})\) Euclidean embedding bound. We then show this is asymptotically tight by realizing every finite tree as the \(s\)-line graph of an \(α\)-acyclic hypergraph. Thus, the worst-case distortion is \(Θ(\sqrt{\log\log n})\), including for hypergraphs of rank at most \(3s+1\).

papers.title: Random Clocks on Computation Paths]{Random Clocks on Computation Paths: How Far Can They Reach, and When Does Stepping Back Help?
papers.abstract: We watch a computation only at moments chosen by a random clock that can leap ahead, pause, or step back, and we count looks rather than steps. How far can such a clock reliably see with polynomially many looks, and does stepping back help? Rare long leaps reach exponential and doubly exponential time, with infinitely many levels between polynomial and exponential time. A clock that tends to fall back sees only the start of the input, and below polynomial time we find infinitely many incomparable levels. Stepping back can help decisively. For clocks whose long leaps occur only at rare positions, no forward-only clock goes beyond polynomial time, while even single steps back raise the reach to exponential time. Stepping back cannot help, however, when the clock's leaps ignore its position.

papers.title: Union of Translates of a Convex Body
papers.abstract: We consider the problem of calculating the volume of the union of translates of a strictly convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^d$. When $K$ is a ball, it is possible to simplify the inclusion-exclusion formula by summing over only a small subset of all terms. This subset corresponds to intersecting cells in the Voronoi diagram of the ball centers. We prove that the same simplification is valid for every strictly convex $K$ if and only if $d\leq 2$. Moreover, in three dimensions and when $K$ is $C^4$, we use the Fubini-Pick affine invariant to show that the topological identity underlying this technique holds if and only if $K$ is an ellipsoid.

papers.title: On Multi-label radio Labelings of Graphs
papers.abstract: We propose and study a multi-labeling generalization of the $k$-radio labeling problem of graphs: given a graph $G$ and integers $k$ and $m$, assign to each vertex of $G$ a set of $m$ integer labels such that distinct labels assigned to a vertex differ by at least $k+1$, and the labels of any two distinct vertices $x$ and $y$ pairwise differ by at least $k+1-d(x,y)$, with $d(x,y)$ being the distance between vertices $x$ and $y$. We prove general bounds on the minimum span of such a labeling and more refined results for the case $k=1$. For paths and cycles, we derive sharp bounds on the minimum span when $k$ is small. We finally propose a conjecture for the minimum span on the path and for an almost-tight bound on the cycle.

papers.title: Bayesian Analysis of Inclusion Transaction Fee Mechanisms with Multiple Concurrent Proposers
papers.abstract: The goal of this paper is to distill insight around the trade-offs present on Bayesian equilibria of transaction fee mechanism (TFM) design under $n$ multiple concurrent proposers (MCP). We conceptualize a technical toolkit that unlocks the analysis of hard-to-characterize equilibria of finite Bayesian MCP TFM games by examining sequences of joint user--proposer mixed equilibria as the number of users increases and keeping the relative congestion $ρ$ that they cause fixed in the sequence limit. We first consider the popular mechanisms of "pay-once" (which charges transactions its bid only once regardless of the duplicate copies that end up being included by proposers) and "pay-per-inclusion" (PPI in short, which charges a transaction for each copy that appears). We prove that PPI is efficient in the limit of equilibria sequences, and incentivizes users to route to only one proposer. We characterize $m$ users' asymptotic behavior in PPI even in finite markets varying with $O(\sqrt{m})$, where we show users in a $Θ(n\sqrt{ρ(1-ρ)/m})$ window near an efficient cutoff exhibit fixed inclusion probability akin to a normal distribution's CDF. We additionally show that on a value-dependent basis, pay-once exhibits a higher degree of duplication and lower probability of inclusion for higher-value transactions than PPI. Pay-once's inefficiency persists even in the large market limit and even in regimes with ample blockspace where all transactions fit across all blocks. We study interpolations between these two mechanisms proving that some higher coefficients (towards PPI) reduce duplication and increase inclusion probability. We then use our tools to show that exclusive proposer payments yield inefficient equilibria (in fact, with maximal possible duplication), even if users still pay multiple times when included more than once and their payment is burnt when non-exclusive.

papers.title: Block basis reduction for linear codes in non-Hamming metrics
papers.abstract: In this paper, we generalize the code basis reduction to non-Hamming metrics. We propose a block basis reduction (BKZ) algorithm for codes that works for all coordinate-additive metrics. Our algorithm is a generalization of the algorithm of Ghentiyala and Stephens-Davidowitz, which in turn is an adaptation of the famous BKZ algorithm for lattices to linear codes and the Hamming metric. For block size~$2$ (LLL), we propose a polynomial-time algorithm with complexity~$\mathcal{O}(n^4 q^3)$ operations in~$\mathbb{F}_q$, where~$n$ is the length of the code and~$q$ is the alphabet size. For the Lee metric we provide an implementation of our algorithms and present experimental results on finding low Lee weight codewords.

papers.title: Ramsey expansions of $S$-metric spaces
papers.abstract: Let $S\subseteq \mathbb R^+$ be a subset of positive reals. We say that a metric space is an $S$-metric space if the range of the metric is a subset of $S\cup \{0\}$. In 2007, Delhommé, Laflamme, Pouzet, and Sauer characterized those sets $S$ for which the class of all finite $S$-metric spaces has the amalgamation property. Given an amalgamation class, a natural question is what its Ramsey expansion is. Ramsey expansions are known for classes of $S$-metric spaces for which $S\cup\{0\}$ carries a natural distance monoid structure, for example for $S=\mathbb Q^+$ or when $S$ is topologically closed. In this paper, we extend this result to all amalgamation classes of finite $S$-metric spaces, thereby completing the Ramsey-theoretic classification of amalgamation classes of finite $S$-metric spaces.
